draft_notes.explanation:
The emitted solver works directly in visible coordinates. It does not undo the D4 transform or the palette. The rule is the same under every D4 map and every palette: split the grid into two halves, then translate each shape so its marker cells land on dots of the same colour. Only the split axis and the translation vectors change in the visible frame, and both are computed from pixels.

(1) Choosing the split. Only even dimensions are candidates. A split is valid when each half's mode colour is absent from the other half. In the true split, the dot-half background, the shape-half background and the body colour each occur in only one half. A wrong split always puts the dot-half background into both halves, so it fails this test. This avoids the archived solver's plurality-based guess, which can fail when large boxes outnumber background cells. If no candidate passes, the solver falls back to the archived left/right-then-top/bottom rule.

(2) Choosing the dot half. It is the half whose non-mode colours all reappear in the other half; each dot colour also appears as a marker in the shape half. The shape half fails this test because its body or background colour is absent from the dot half. The archived check that every dot is an isolated pixel is not used, because the generator can place markers next to each other.

(3) Colour roles from pixels.
- Shape background: among shape-half colours absent from the dot half, the one whose complement splits into solid rectangles. The generator keeps boxes rectangular and separated by gaps.
- Body colour: the colour absent from the dot half that occurs in every shape. This is used instead of a per-shape majority, which fails for 2x2 boxes with 3 markers.
- Markers: all non-body cells of a shape.

(4) Placement as an exact cover. Each shape's candidate offsets anchor its first marker on a same-colour dot. An offset is kept only if every marker hits a same-colour dot, every body cell lands on dot-half background inside the grid, and boxes keep the generator's one-cell gap. A backtracking search tries shapes with more markers first and tries placing before skipping, as the archived greedy order does. It looks for a set of placements whose markers cover every dot exactly once.
- If that finds nothing, it retries without the in-bounds, background and gap checks.
- If that also fails, it uses the archived greedy procedure.

The output is the dot half's size and background with the chosen shapes painted at their offsets, clipped at the edges. d4 and palette are recorded as constants only: the generator draws the split axis and all colours at random anyway, so roles must be inferred per grid.
draft_notes.limitations:
Nothing has been run; no fixtures or fresh samples were tested.

Constructor ambiguities that need host review:
- **Coincidental extra fits.** Dot colours may repeat across boxes, and there are 1-marker shapes. A marker pattern can therefore sometimes fit the dots at more than one offset, or two different sets of placements can each cover all dots exactly. In these rare cases the generator's answer is not determined by the visible grid. The solver returns the first cover in a fixed order (more-marker shapes first, dots in reading order). That reading order depends on orientation, so outputs could differ across D4 variants in such scenes, as they would for the archived solver.
- **Archived solver mismatches.** The archived greedy solver may disagree with the generator when markers are adjacent, or when a 2x2 box has a marker majority. These are not new puzzle rules; this solver handles both cases.

Assumptions that come from the generator, not from the visible rule:
- The two halves are exactly equal in size along an even dimension.
- Boxes do not reach the full width or height of a half.
- Any two boxes are separated by at least one empty row or one empty column.

If a case breaks these assumptions, the colour-role and split inference falls back to heuristics: mode colours, the archived split rule, or greedy placement.

I found no contradiction between the fixtures and the uniform rule.
